opus-5.5.text:
When I joined the preparedness team, the big shift we were anticipating was that models were going to start thinking for longer before they answered. That changes the risk picture quite a bit. A model that can reason through a multi-step problem, check its own work, and try different approaches is a very different thing to evaluate than one that just produces a quick response.

So a lot of my early thinking was about whether our evaluations were actually measuring the right things. Many of the benchmarks at the time were getting saturated. Models were doing well on multiple-choice-style questions, but that didn't tell us much about whether they could, say, help someone carry out a complex biology protocol or find and exploit a real vulnerability in a codebase. With reasoning models, you expect capabilities to jump in exactly those long-horizon, multi-step areas. We needed evals that were harder, more realistic, and closer to the actual tasks we were worried about.

That meant building things like more agentic evaluations, tasks where the model has to plan, use tools, and recover from mistakes, and working closely with domain experts to design problems that couldn't be solved by pattern matching or memorization. We wanted early warning signals, so we'd see capabilities coming before they arrived rather than after.

The other piece was being honest that we didn't fully know what these models would be capable of. So we tried to build the process to be adaptive: run evaluations throughout training rather than only at the end, have clear thresholds for what counts as medium or high risk in each category, and make sure the right mitigations were ready to go if we crossed one. Preparedness, to me, was really about not being surprised. If a model is going to be meaningfully more capable, you want to have already done the work to understand it before it's in people's hands.

r001.rationale: The response frames preparation around anticipating longer reasoning and future capability jumps, and building evaluations to detect those capabilities before they arrive.

fable-5.1.text:
When I joined the preparedness team, the honest answer is that we didn't yet know what the models were going to be good at, so the first thing I did was try to figure out how to measure them. Reasoning models were just starting to come online internally, and you could feel that something was shifting. Models that would previously fail on a hard chemistry or biology question, or on a multi-step coding task, were suddenly getting partway there. So the question became: how do we know when "partway there" turns into "actually dangerous"?

My background is in medicine and research, so I came at it from the angle of, what would a real expert actually be able to do with this? A lot of the early benchmarks were basically trivia. You could ask a model a factual question and it would nail it, but that doesn't tell you much about whether it could help someone walk through a wet-lab protocol or troubleshoot a failed experiment. So we spent a lot of time building evaluations that looked more like real work: long-horizon tasks, tacit knowledge, the kind of things that are hard to look up.

The other thing we tried to be disciplined about was setting thresholds before we saw the results. It's very tempting to look at a model's score and then decide what it means. We wanted the opposite, to say in advance, "if a model crosses this line in bio or cyber, here's what we're committing to do," and then let the data tell us where we are. That's really the spirit of the Preparedness Framework.

And then practically, it meant running the evals early and often. Not waiting until a model was finished, but testing checkpoints as they trained so we'd have warning rather than surprise. With reasoning models in particular, we learned that capability could jump quickly with more test-time compute, so we had to think about evaluating the model at its strongest, not just its default. That was a real mindset change for the team.

r001.rationale: The response describes measuring emerging capabilities before their risks were clear, testing checkpoints early, and assessing reasoning models at their strongest as capabilities develop.

astra-6.text:
The way I thought about it was: we need to prepare for capabilities we haven’t yet seen, rather than assume the next model will look like the last one. With reasoning models, that means asking what changes when a model can spend more time working through a problem, and whether our evaluations would actually pick up those changes.

So I’d start with the risks we’re concerned about, work backward to the capabilities that could enable them, and ask how we could test those capabilities meaningfully. The goal is to get useful evidence early enough that it can inform decisions about safeguards and deployment, while being honest about what our tests don’t tell us.

r001.rationale: The response says to prepare for capabilities not yet seen and not assume the next model will resemble the last, applying that approach to reasoning models.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I thought about it was: how do we prepare for capabilities we haven’t yet seen? With reasoning models, you can’t just look at what a model does in a quick interaction. You also have to ask what it can do when it has more time to work through a problem, or when it can use tools and take multiple steps.

So I approached it as a measurement problem. What capabilities would matter from a risk perspective? How would we test for them, and how would we know whether our tests were actually challenging enough? Then, as we learned more about the models, we’d need to update those evaluations. The goal was to get useful evidence early enough that it could inform decisions about safeguards and deployment.

r001.rationale: The response frames preparation as asking how to prepare for capabilities not yet seen and how models might perform with more time or tools.
